title: Performance Metric Relationships
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Software Architecture
description: Move arrival rate, service time, and concurrency limit sliders to see how throughput, response time, queue depth, and p50/p95/p99 latency are tied together by Little's Law, and what happens when the queue saturates.

educational.topic: Latency, throughput, concurrency, and Little's Law
learningObjectives: Students will be able to use Little's Law to relate arrival rate, response time, and the number of requests in a system, and predict when a concurrency limit saturates and tail latency grows.
prerequisites: Concurrency limits such as thread or connection pools

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Parameter exploration with predict-then-check against a live calculation
keyQuestions: How many workers does this workload need on average, and how much headroom does the limit leave?
Why does p99 grow so much faster than p50 as utilization rises?
What are the two levers for reducing response time, according to Little's Law?
commonMisconceptions: A system at 90% utilization still has 10% to spare (waiting time is already growing steeply).
Average response time describes what users experience (the tail can be several times the median).
Throughput keeps rising with load (it is capped at capacity once the system saturates).
assessmentOpportunities: Give students a response measure (for example, "p95 response time under 200 ms at 300 requests per second") and a 60 ms service time. Ask for the offered load, the minimum concurrency that is stable, a limit that meets the measure in this model, and the assumption they would most want to verify with a load test.
